A **sample** is a piece of a recording reused in a new piece of music. It can be one drum hit, a bar of a drum break, a chord from
an old soul record, a word from a film, or a whole chorus. Hip-hop was built on samples; so were house, jungle, much of pop since
the 1990s, and every DJ set ever played.

## Three sizes of sample

- **One-shot**: a single sound (a kick, a snare, a horn stab, "Ahh"). You play it from a pad or key; it lasts as long as it lasts.
- **Loop**: one, two or four bars that repeat seamlessly. A loop has a tempo (BPM) and usually a key.
- **Phrase**: a longer piece (a sung line, a riff, a speech) placed once, not looped.

A **break** is a special loop: the moment in a funk or soul record when everything drops out but the drums. DJ Kool Herc played two
copies of the same record in the Bronx in the 1970s and switched between them to stretch the break out for dancers: the "merry-go-round"
that started hip-hop. The most sampled break is probably the Winstons' "Amen, Brother" (1969), the basis of jungle and drum and bass.

## Two ways to use a sample

| | The producer | The DJ |
|---|---|---|
| Where the sample lives | Inside a new track (a DAW, an MPC, an SP-404) | On a record, a USB stick or a laptop, played live |
| What changes it | Chopping, re-pitching, re-sequencing, effects | Mixing, EQ, loops, cue points, scratching |
| The result | A new recording | A performance (a set, a mix) |
| Typical material | Breaks, one-shots, chords, vocal phrases | Whole songs, **acapellas** (vocals only), **instrumentals**, **edits** |

The two overlap more every year: DJ software can loop, slice and separate a song into stems live, and producers make "DJ tools"
(intros, edits, loops) for other DJs to play.

## Hear a loop, then pieces of it

The sampler below has a two-bar drum break loaded (made on this site, so it is free to use). Press **▶ Whole loop** to hear
it, then click the pads: each plays one of 16 equal slices. The waveform shows where each slice starts.

<div class="sp-pads" data-id="sp-what" data-loop="demo:break100" data-show="wave pads library"></div>

1. Find the pads that hold a **kick**, a **snare** and a **hi-hat**. Those are one-shots cut out of a loop.
2. Play the pads in order, 1 to 16, steadily. You have rebuilt the loop by hand.
3. Now play 1, 1, 5, 1, 1, 1, 5, 7. The same sounds, a new rhythm: that is sampling in one sentence.

## A loop on a deck

A DJ hears the same material as a whole. Press **▶** on the deck, then pull the **pitch fader**: the loop speeds up *and*
its pitch rises, like a record on a faster turntable. Drag the label on the platter to move the record by hand.

<div class="dj-tt" data-id="dj-what" data-decks="1" data-a="demo:soul84" data-show="decks library"></div>

## What makes a good sample

- **Space**: a few bars where one instrument plays alone, or the drums play alone, are easier to reuse than a full mix.
- **A clean start**: a hit right on the beat makes a loop that lines up.
- **Character**: tape hiss, room sound and a drummer's swing are part of why producers sample old records rather than programming drums.

Every sample of someone else's recording also raises a question of permission: [Sampling 6](sampling-law.qmd) is about that.
